articles.title_orig: China upgrades trade deal with Peru as Washington struggles to preserve US domination of South America
articles.title_zh: China upgrades trade deal with Peru as Washington struggles to preserve US domination of South America
articles.content_orig:
`China’s upgraded free trade agreement with Peru, which entered into force on November 1, is another setback for Washington’s attempt to reassert its domination over Latin America through Trump’s “Donroe Doctrine.”
Peru has become a strategic battleground in the growing conflict between declining US imperialism and China’s expanding economic power.
China buys more than one-third of Peru’s exports, and its investments in copper mining and the Chancay megaport are transforming South America’s economic relations with Asia. Unable to reverse this through economic competition, Washington increasingly resorts to political interference, intimidation and military pressure.
The struggle over Peru exposes the fundamental contradiction between the international development of the productive forces and the nation-state system, which inevitably leads to war as Washington seeks to preserve its political and military supremacy over an entire hemisphere and the world.
In 2025, Peru exported US$32.6 billion in goods to China, 36.2 percent of its total exports, compared with US$10.15 billion, or 11.3 percent, to the United States. China is also Peru’s largest supplier, accounting for nearly 29 percent of imports in 2024.
Washington, which historically regarded Latin America as its exclusive sphere of influence, confronts a direct challenge from China, whose industrial expansion has created enormous demand for copper, iron ore and other strategic minerals.
The Chinese-controlled Chancay megaport marks a qualitative advance in this process. Inaugurated in November 2024, its first phase involved an investment of approximately US$1.3 billion. Between January and July 2026 the port handled 246,452 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU), nearly 75 percent more than a year earlier.
Even more significant is the proposed transcontinental railway linking Brazil’s Atlantic coast with Peru’s Pacific coast, which would make Chancay a major outlet for South American agricultural and mineral exports bound for Asia, bypassing routes long dominated by US interests. Washington’s opposition is therefore not directed merely against individual Chinese investments. It seeks to prevent the emergence of an integrated South American infrastructure oriented toward Asia.
The Trump administration’s National Security Strategy vows to “deny non-Hemispheric competitors” control of strategically vital assets in the hemisphere. In a September 8 op-ed in Lima’s El Comercio , ahead of his visit, Secretary of State Marco Rubio accused Beijing of entering the region with “promises that hide predatory practices.” The Chinese Embassy replied that the Western Hemisphere is “no one’s backyard.” On September 10, beside Rubio, President Keiko Fujimori confirmed Peru’s entry into the US-led “Shield of the Americas.”
This policy did not begin with Trump. For the November 2024 APEC summit in Lima, attended by President Joe Biden, the Peruvian Congress authorized the entry of 600 armed US Army, Air Force and Marine Corps personnel, with aircraft, refueling tankers, helicopters and sniper rifles, deployed not only in Lima but in Pisco and Chiclayo. Officially there for summit security, the deployment demonstrated Washington’s ability to project armed force into Peru under the cover of a diplomatic gathering. Congress has since authorized the presence of US military personnel in Peru throughout 2026.
In Panama, the Supreme Court in January annulled the concessions held by Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison at its two main ports. In Venezuela, Washington showed its readiness to use direct military force with the January 2026 operation that seized President Nicolás Maduro. Venezuelan oil exports to China have stopped as Washington has asserted control over the country’s petroleum reserves, the largest on the planet.
Peru is a more complicated problem. Chancay is majority-owned by the Chinese state enterprise COSCO Shipping, and any attempt to dislodge Chinese capital would threaten vital interests of Peru’s own ruling class.
Washington’s pressure came into the open in April 2026, when interim President José María Balcázar tried to postpone the purchase of 24 Lockheed Martin F-16 Block 70 fighters, a program worth about US$3.5 billion. Peru’s own technical evaluation committee had ranked the French Rafale first and the Swedish Gripen second, with the F-16 third.
On April 17, hours before a scheduled signing, Balcázar said the decision should be left to the government taking office on July 28. US Ambassador Bernie Navarro replied the same day that anyone dealing with the United States “in bad faith” could expect Washington to “use every available tool” against them.
Within a week the matter was settled over the president’s head. The first contract, for 12 aircraft worth US$1.54 billion, was signed in a closed ceremony at Las Palmas Air Base on April 20. On April 22, Balcázar’s foreign and defense ministers resigned, accusing him of lying about the deal’s status, and the next day the Finance Ministry transferred a first payment of US$462 million.
The episode exposed what Peruvian “sovereignty” amounts to. In a country with enormous deficits in education, health, housing and infrastructure, billions have been committed to aircraft whose purpose the Heritage Foundation stated plainly: the purchase shows Peru’s “commitment to greater interoperability with U.S. forces.” Peru’s air force is being integrated into Washington’s preparations for war with China.
Washington’s influence over the Peruvian state was evident in the removal of President Pedro Castillo in December 2022. On December 6, US Ambassador Lisa Kenna, a nine-year CIA veteran, met with Defense Minister Gustavo Bobbio, a retired army general sworn in the day before. On December 7, Castillo announced the dissolution of Congress. Bobbio resigned within hours, the armed forces and police refused to back the president, Congress removed him, and he was arrested that afternoon.
What was discussed has never been disclosed. But the ambassador’s contact with the defense minister on the eve of the crisis, followed by Washington’s rapid condemnation of Castillo and recognition of the succession, shows the weight of US ties to the Peruvian state at the decisive moment.
Washington kept close relations with Castillo’s successor, Dina Boluarte, as her killed dozens of protesters, above all in Peru’s predominantly Indigenous south.
The Peruvian ruling class confronts a contradiction that cannot be resolved through declarations of neutrality. Its economic interests increasingly depend on China, while its military and political institutions are tied to Washington.
Luis Miguel Castilla, a former economy minister and former ambassador in Washington, said that Fujimori’s approach showed “she is going to be pragmatic,” adding that this “has been part of our foreign policy for a long time.”
But what does such pragmatism mean when Washington demands the exclusion of Chinese companies from strategic infrastructure? Chinese firms have invested heavily in copper, electricity, transportation and ports, and their influence cannot be eliminated by decree without threatening the profits of powerful sections of Peru’s capitalist class. At the same time, that class depends upon the military, police and judicial institutions through which its property and rule are maintained. It tries to profit from both powers, but as their rivalry grows more militarist, that balancing act is becoming impossible.
The United States, despite its relative economic decline, retains overwhelming military power and a worldwide network of bases. Its determination to preserve its supremacy creates the danger that economic competition will be settled by military means. Peru’s location, mineral wealth and ties to China place it in the direct path of this confrontation. The struggle between the great powers could bring military conflict onto Latin America and Peruvian territory, with devastating consequences for its population.
Nei

articles.title_orig: British women receive pardons for past abortion convictions
articles.title_zh: British women receive pardons for past abortion convictions
articles.content_orig:
Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales .
Ending the Victorian-era law should avoid traumatic experiences such as that of Nicola Packer, who was recently cleared by a jury after taking medication at home during a Covid lockdown. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was around 26 weeks pregnant, far beyond the legal 10 week limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge told the BBC's Today Programme she had been "treated appallingly" until justice was served.
Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalisation amendment last year, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who have been "unnecessarily harmed" by an "outdated" law.
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.
Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.
Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.
Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".
"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.
"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."
Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.
"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."
It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."
At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.
It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.
Women affected do not need to take any action.
Minister for Victims and Tackling Violence Against Women and Girls, Alex Davies-Jones, said pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy had been a priority.
"I'm pleased to be able to commence the change that Parliament voted for.
"For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team."
Heidi Stewart, from the abortion care provider BPAS, said: "While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice."
Abortion in England and Wales is legal with an authorised provider up to 24 weeks, with very limited circumstances allowing one after this time, such as when the mother's life is at risk or the child would be born with a severe disability.
It is also legal to take prescribed medication at home if a woman is less than 10 weeks pregnant.

articles.title_orig: Trump heads to Asia for historic nuclear talks with China and Russia
articles.title_zh: Trump heads to Asia for historic nuclear talks with China and Russia
articles.content_orig:
Washington — President Trump set off Monday for a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
Ahead of his departure, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.
The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first between the three leaders , is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.
Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.
The president will first head to the Philippines, where the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is being held. Mr. Trump will meet with Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.
On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.
As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking. Mr. Trump is not expected to speak about the 4 1/2-year war in Ukraine during the summit.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang , the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.
Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.
"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.
When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Both Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.
Seiji  Yamashita contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: Trump administration orders Commerce to close chip loophole at heart of Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration said on Monday that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. chips through the use of data centers outside China’s borders.
The rule aims to close what many in Washington see as a loophole allowing China to sidestep a ban that prevents Chinese firms from buying the most advanced A.I. chips made by companies like Nvidia. Chinese firms have continued to legally access the chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. Whether to close the loophole has been a significant source of contention within the Trump administration.
The new rule is intended to make it harder for Chinese firms to remotely access the chips. It will require overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in a small group of high-risk countries, a list that includes China, Russia and Iran.
Data centers are also required to perform strict checks on their customers to determine if they are linked to those countries. And the U.S. will now require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said.
The provision, which goes into effect in 90 days, will “undermine” the ability of companies in those countries from using U.S. chips to train advanced A.I. models, the administration said in a news release.
The plan to crack down on China’s ability to access the coveted A.I. chips comes as President Trump is scheduled to travel to Asia. He will travel to the Philippines and then to China for an economic summit, where he is expected to meet with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping and discuss the war in Iran, nuclear nonproliferation and trade. The data center rules could create a new source of friction between the countries, at a time when Mr. Trump has been trying to keep a fragile trade truce with China intact.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.title_zh: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.content_orig:
Airports were thrown into chaos, with hundreds of flights canceled and thousands of travelers stranded. A Federal Aviation Administration investigation soon traced the disaster to an unlikely source: A router that had locked up the nation’s air traffic control network.
That incident happened 17 years ago – leading to urgent calls for FAA upgrades.
Yet on Friday, an eerily similar scene played out, this time with a rare nationwide halt to all flights as communications with pilots broke down.
Once again, the FAA now suspects the problems began with a single router, newly installed in a remote radio outpost in Arkansas.
While federal investigators with the FBI and FAA are still working to untangle exactly what went wrong last week – and who is to blame – the similar 2009 incident is a startling illustration of how long US officials have battled to upgrade an aging flight control network.
A CNN review of government oversight reports and past incidents vividly shows how decades of warnings about the FAA’s aging infrastructure have failed to head off the kind of mass outages that again struck America’s aviation industry on Friday.
“We’ve known the system has been antiquated for many years,” said Margaret Wallace, an assistant professor of aviation management at the Florida Institute of Technology. “Much of what was there can almost date back to World War II.”
The Trump administration has touted its plans to speedily replace antiquated copper wiring with fiber optics and newer equipment and pointed to Friday’s outage as evidence that Congress needs to provide more than the $12.5 billion already earmarked for upgrades.
“Congress did give me $12.5 billion, but they were very specific on how we spend it,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday . “I have no money for a new network. I don’t have any new money to build new software to separate planes in the air space.”
But Friday’s incident, which Duffy said occurred during one of those upgrades, has also sharpened questions about how effectively the administration and its key contractors are carrying out the improvements already in progress.
Similar concerns were raised in September in a US Government Accountability Office report warning the FAA could potentially cause more breakdowns by moving too hastily in efforts to modernize its systems.
The report stated the FAA had made progress in replacing thousands of old copper wires with high-speed fiber optic cables but also expressed concern that the agency had not effectively scheduled those replacements to “reduce impacts to controller operations.”
“FAA could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions,” stated the GAO report , which added, “If these risks are realized, FAA would need to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more flight delays and safety incidents.”
The infrastructure that keeps thousands of flights safely separated in US airspace is built on a network of comparatively ancient technology – from copper phone lines to old computers, all of which must link a complex nationwide network of air traffic controllers.
Government officials have long sounded alarms about breakdowns in that system, which at times has failed spectacularly.
In 2009, an FAA telecommunications outage affected more than 100 air traffic facilities and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.
A review by the Department of Transportation’s inspector general later found a technician had “incorrectly configured” a router, which caused an improper flow of air traffic data that blocked much of the system.
The technician described in the IG’s report worked for Harris Corporation, which later merged with another business to form L3Harris, the contractor now under scrutiny for the latest outage.
An FAA review panel later recommended a spate of improvements in the wake of that mass outage, including looking into setting up new backup systems.
Eight years later, though, the FAA’s inspector general warned that technology disruptions were still a major threat to the nation’s air travel – citing a number of other recent failures, including a fire in Chicago and a flood in Texas that disabled control towers for long periods of time.
“Significant work remains to mitigate the impact of air traffic control disruptions,” the 2017 report found .
In 2023, the FAA briefly halted all domestic flight departures after another  outage. A subsequent GAO report found many air traffic control systems were increasingly prone to failures and relied on hard-to-find spare parts.
The assessment determined that more than a third of the systems were “unsustainable,” with others heading in the same direction. That same year, a safety review team explicitly warned of potential communication failures due to aging infrastructure and budgetary constraints, telling the FAA in a report that “risk could quickly reach unacceptable levels.”
Last year, a series of disruptions prompted more scrutiny. Outages at a Philadelphia control facility caused the FAA to halt flights at Newark Liberty International Airport. A controller who spoke with CNN anonymously at the time said a single data feed connecting two facilities – similar to an extension cord-like line – had crashed at least twice.
Following the outages, federal investigators questioned whether the FAA had adequately assessed the reliability of telecommunications lines before relocating Newark’s airspace management from New York to Philadelphia. An IG report described a “burnt copper wire” and “failures of both primary and redundant communication infrastructure.”
President Donald Trump’s mega-spending bill passed by Republicans last year included $12.5 billion to start widespread upgrades to the FAA’s infrastructure, a plan Duffy touted at an aviation summit in April.
He said half of the system’s old wires had already been replaced. He referenced the incidents in Newark and blamed outdated wires, stating that since those had been replaced Newark had some of the “most on-time performance.”
“In one year, this administration has done more in replacing old wires than the last administration did in all four of their years,” Duffy told the audience.
Yet the GAO’s September report struck a more cautious note about those plans and criticized the FAA for not having detailed cost estimate and integration plans around its new air traffic control system.
Without doing so, it would “increase the likelihood of FAA repeating its history of cost overruns, delays, and unmet performance targets,” the report found.
The latest mass outage to America’s air traffic control system began as a result of implementing those new upgrades, officials now believe.
Duffy said at a news conference that L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from copper wires to fiber optics prior to the outage.
After the contractor installed a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas, the device started pinging the FAA networks at a rapid rate on Friday afternoon, according to an FAA statement. A second router in Texas experienced similar issues. The FAA disabled both routers and approximately 60 others as a precaution.
The FAA says that during the outage, 17 of its 22 air route traffic control centers experienced problems.
A telecommunications router suspected of playing a role in the disruption has been sent to a testing facility in Florida, according to a senior administration official.
The FAA and L3Harris are investigating whether the failure was caused by a defective router or an installation or configuration error. The FBI is also involved out of an abundance of caution, the official said.
In a statement, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s investigation and noted the company had already completed more than 70% of the conversion from copper wires to fiber optics.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Asia trip: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, nuclear summit with Xi and Putin, maybe Kim meeting
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Asia trip: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, nuclear summit with Xi and Putin, maybe Kim meeting
articles.content_orig:
China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.
That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.
While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.
"For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.
Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.
The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda.
"He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world , whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call . The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.
China has no interest in engaging in nuclear disarmament talks until it achieves parity with the U.S. in about 10 years, said David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy.
Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.
The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, said Roche, while Trump's political standing slides. Nvidia and the chip-smuggling issues involving a suspected Chinese spy will stay off the agenda, as Trump steers clear of thorny issues where he is unlikely to claim success.
China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.
China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement.
"Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability."
A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.
Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.
U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

A major week for Wall Street started on a down note. US markets closed lower Monday, led by declines in technology stocks associated with the artificial intelligence boom.
The S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739 points, or 1.4%. Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, surged 19%.
Shares of Nvidia ( NVDA ) dropped 4.1%, falling for the third consecutive day since Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia shares are coming off their worst week in 19 months. Investors are gearing up for Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, expected Tuesday after the market close.
Shares of the semiconductor chip designer have had a rocky few weeks, with the Huang scandal accelerating declines. Nvidia shares are down roughly 35% since a record high on October 6, erasing about $2 trillion in market value.
On Monday, shares of Nvidia closed at $156.14, their lowest level since July 1, 2025. Nvidia shares have erased all of their gains over the past 16 months. Nvidia stock was hit by a raft of Wall Street analysts slashing their price targets last week. At Evercore ISI, analysts cut their price target to $186, down from a prior target of $465. At HSBC, analysts cut their target to $170, down from $365.
Shares of semiconductor chipmakers, Big Tech and other companies involved in the data center buildout fell Monday. Intel shares ( INTC ) fell 7.1%, while Alphabet shares ( GOOG ) fell 3.85%. CoreWeave shares ( CRWV ) sank 6.1%.
The Commerce Department on Monday also tightened export controls designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips. The much-anticipated Commerce rule puts new curbs on US exports to data centers that provide “significant volumes” of computing to companies based in countries subject to US arms embargoes, such as China, Iran and Russia.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gained more than 2% last week. The declines on Monday ate away at those gains. Overall, the S&P and Nasdaq are down roughly 5% and 11%, respectively, since record highs on October 6. The Dow is down 5% since its peak on August 5.
Investors are also gearing up for Anthropic’s expected initial public offering later this week. The AI frontier lab is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion , and its IPO is a pivotal moment for the tech boom that has become a driving force for the US stock market.
“How investors view Nvidia’s updates against the recent turmoil left in the wake of Jensen Huang’s departure and the market reaction to Anthropic becoming a public company may determine whether the AI trade can gain its footing or whether hiccups here cause further damage across the ecosystem,” Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, wrote in a Monday note.

articles.title_orig: White House "tiger team" formed to prevent another nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: White House "tiger team" formed to prevent another nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
Days after a debilitating nationwide ground stop, the Trump administration’s push for emergency funding for the nation’s aging air traffic control system is running into resistance from top Republicans on Capitol Hill.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued an urgent demand this weekend for as much as $50 billion after halted flights left over a million passengers stranded on Friday.
But key Republicans – including Senate Majority Leader John Thune – are demanding more information about that request, including what the administration had done with the last sizable tranche of funding meant to upgrade those air systems. And few lawmakers believe the GOP-led Congress will be able to deliver that money in the final weeks of their power, before the Democratic takeover begins in January.
“I think it’s highly unlikely that Congress is just going to write a check for $50 billion just because he says so,” GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said of Duffy’s request.
He added that any push to spend that kind of money – a sum that rivals the annual appropriations for many government departments – would need far more time to win approval from Congress.
“When you do things really fast around here, you make mistakes. And that’s why the whole system is designed to move methodically and deliberatively,” Cornyn warned.
Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to update air traffic control systems as part of President Donald Trump’s massive spending and policy bill – which many lawmakers, including Thune, have argued has not yet been fully spent.
“About $8 billion of that [is] still sitting around,” Thune said on Monday of the initial $12.5 billion tranche. “I mean there’s some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is,” he added, arguing Congress has “attempted to do what we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization” are answered.
Others in GOP leadership are privately baffled — or even frustrated — by Duffy’s attempt to blame Congress for a funding shortfall, despite Republicans doling out billions last year, according to multiple sources. Republicans aren’t ruling out more money for air traffic modernization — a decades-long priority for both parties. But they’re making clear that they won’t simply rubber stamp $50 billion – or any amount – without clarity from the White House about where the money has gone so far.
“What I think a lot of people don’t realize is that the FAA has not spent the money that we previously appropriated — and that part of that money was designated to beautify airports. That should not be the priority. We do have a serious problem with our air traffic control system,” said GOP Sen. Susan Collins, a top Senate appropriator who said she was briefed over the weekend by the FAA administrator.
But, of the request for more funding, she said: “I don’t see the justification yet for that much.”
Another reason for the hesitation in Congress: Lawmakers are not entirely clear on what happened to ground flights on Friday. Some key lawmakers will briefed behind closed doors on Tuesday. And Duffy will meet with Senate Republicans over lunch on Capitol Hill, according to a source familiar.
“Well, we gave them $12.5 billion,” Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, a member of GOP leadership, said when asked about Duffy’s finger-pointing at Congress amid fallout over the decision to ground flights.
Duffy has said though that his agency does not have the funding it needs.
“I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom. I can’t build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s, but there’s no money for that. There’s no money for towers. Our towers are old,” Duffy said on CNN’s “State of the Union” with Dana Bash on Sunday.
According to a source familiar with the plans, DOT has “allocated” all of the $12.5 billion to certain projects. However, the money is not deemed “spent” until those specific projects are installed and operational. Several of the DOT’s plans are underway, the source said. Duffy has publicly stated the $12.5 billion will be spent by the end of December 2028.
According to a fact sheet from the department, “Congress placed parameters on the funding outlining exactly how much of the total package could be spent on specific categories of work. The Department does not have the legal flexibility to move funds from one workstream to another,” the release states.
“As the Department has made clear for the last two years – separate funding is needed to cover separate work streams,” it states, citing efforts such as modernizing the digital architecture powering air traffic control and upgrading and replacing aviation infrastructure.
GOP Sen. Rand Paul repeatedly called for an accounting of where the $12.5 billion has gone. “I think a methodical look at what happened, what mistakes were made, where the money is being spent, before we just immediately throw more money at the problem,” he said.
GOP Sen. John Kennedy made clear he wants Duffy to explain why they need the money. “I want him to sit me down and explain to me what happened and the problem, like he’s talking to a moderately intelligent ninth grader.”
“Then I want him to explain how it’s going to be fixed, when it’s going to be fixed, who’s going to fix it, and how much it’s going to cost,” he said.
As of June, the agency had spent only $474.9 million of the $12.5 billion Congress had appropriated, according to data from a congressional source shared with CNN.
Congress appropriated $1.9 billion to specifically help build a new air traffic control center, for example, but none of that money had been spent by the agency as of June, the source told CNN.
The data shared with CNN shows that the FAA had $4.75 billion dedicated to telecommunications infrastructure and that only $309 million had been spent as of June.
At least one Republican said he has been rattled by a string of high-profile outages across the US – including that nationwide ground stop – and wants to probe whether any of the incidents are related.
“I want a deeper dive. I think we too quickly dismissed that there was no malicious acts,” Sen. Tim Sheehy, a former Navy SEAL and combat veteran, said on Monday. “We had Microsoft go down on Thursday, air traffic go down on Friday, banks go down today. We have very sophisticated digital adversaries. That sounds a little too much of a coincidence to me. So before we dismiss that, I want to see the details on that.”
GOP Sen. Rick Scott of Florida, another senator with some of the nation’s busiest airports in his state, was noncommittal on whether he’d approve the funding.
“I think we have to get all the facts before we do anything…seeing how they’re going to use it,” Scott said. “We have to have a budget and what the timeline is, who’s going to do it, all that.”
CNN’s Ellis Kim and Alexandra Skores contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: ‘It’s a horrible idea’: Republicans shut down talk of Jensen Huang’s return
articles.title_zh: ‘It’s a horrible idea’: Republicans shut down talk of Jensen Huang’s return
articles.content_orig:
Bill Ackman said there could be a case for reinstating Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO — that is, only if Huang is cleared of any wrongdoing related to putting his company's national security obligations at risk.
At a conference hosted by Semafor on Monday, the billionaire activist investor was asked what strategy he would use to pressure the board into reinstating Huang.
Huang resigned from his role on Thursday following the disclosure of extramarital affairs and concerns that he may have been a target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
Ackman said that if Huang's relationships were determined to be a "personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy," there could be a "powerful case" for putting Huang back in the CEO seat, though the investor said it would be "unlikely" for him to be involved in such an effort.
"You just present the facts, and you call a special meeting," he said, adding that an activist investor could also partner with Huang, who owns more than 3% of the company.
Said special meeting would be a shareholder vote on reinstating Huang. The now-former CEO's involvement would not only help the company meet the threshold for calling one — which requires at least 15% of the voting power — but also send a public message that the founder wants to return.
"You call a special meeting, the writing will be on the wall very quickly, I would expect, at which point you don't even have to go the meeting," Ackman said. "Just put him back in, make some changes to the board, and push forward."
A spokesperson for Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.
Ackman, who has defended Huang since the Nvidia founder's affairs were publicized, said the situation is an "interesting activist setup," given that Huang is a heralded founder who would have plenty of shareholder support .

"I think the only cloud is there is some legal uncertainty about what actually went down," Ackman said. "It would be helpful to know that answer before you pursue that."

articles.title_orig: Trump Backs Huang Comeback While Nvidia Board Seeks New CEO
articles.title_zh: Trump Backs Huang Comeback While Nvidia Board Seeks New CEO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Something pretty remarkable is happening in Silicon Valley right now. One shouldn't be surprised, considering the profit motives of many invested in the AI ecosystem and that what Nvidia ( NVDA ) does lies at the center of it all.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as the company's CEO under a cloud of controversy he created, and suddenly some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley are organizing a campaign to bring him back.
Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk has signed on to the "Bring Jensen Back" petition. Other prominent executives have joined, including Uber ( UBER ) founder Travis Kalanick — who left Uber unceremoniously after his own string of highly publicized missteps.
Read more: Live updates on Nvidia ahead of the AI chip titan's earnings
The online petition has attracted more than 180,000 signatures. Nvidia employees have also taken to X and LinkedIn to voice their support for Huang.
Let's be clear: Jensen Huang is an extraordinary entrepreneur . A once-in-a-lifetime type of talent. He helped build Nvidia into one of the world's most important companies, with a market cap that neared $5 trillion earlier this year. His impact on the AI revolution is enormous and will not be forgotten.
But here's the issue a lot of people are right to point out: Being a brilliant CEO does not make you untouchable.
Huang admitted to being unfaithful to Lori, his wife of more than 40 years. There are serious questions surrounding his relationship with a reported Chinese spy. Additional reports say Jensen had affairs with two Nvidia employees, one of whom, Kimberly Powell , was a direct report.
All of these allegations and the broader circumstances deserve a thorough, independent investigation by the board and the law firm leading it, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. They should not be treated as proven facts.
And that's precisely the point.
This isn't just about one man's personal life. It's about corporate governance, national security, the responsibilities of a CEO, and the standards expected of someone running one of America's most strategically important companies.
Nvidia's board has a responsibility to shareholders, employees, and the country — not to Silicon Valley's celebrity CEO culture.
Jensen Huang absolutely deserves due process. But he is not bigger than Nvidia. And no CEO, no matter how brilliant, should be.

articles.title_orig: The Important Gmail Security Settings You Should Be Using
articles.title_zh: The Important Gmail Security Settings You Should Be Using
articles.content_orig:
Having your Google account compromised can be a huge deal.
Gmail is no longer just an email service. Plenty of websites and apps let you log in with your Google account, and many people use that one login for almost everything they do online. It makes signing in a lot easier. It also means that whoever holds the keys to your account holds a lot more than just your private emails.
Google is very aware of that, which is why it offers a variety of security and privacy settings to keep your account safe and keep third parties out of it. These are some of the most important ones you should be using.
Start with Security Checkup ; it's a page in your Google Account that gives you personalized recommendations, like adding a recovery phone number and email. Those might sound like very basic steps, but they matter more than you might think: Google uses them to alert you to suspicious activity and to help you get back in if someone locks you out. From google.com, click your profile icon in the upper right, then click Manage your Google Account . Click Security & sign-in . At the top of the page, you'll see an icon. A green shield means nothing needs your attention right now. A blue, yellow or red exclamation mark means there's something to fix.
The single biggest fix is two-step verification, also known as two-factor authentication. With it on, a stolen password isn't enough, because signing in also takes something you physically have on you, like your phone or your own computer. To switch it on, go to Security & sign-in , find the How you sign in to Google section, select Turn on 2-Step Verification and follow the prompts.
Then there are passkeys, which let you sign in with your fingerprint, face scan or screen lock instead of a password. A passkey can't be shared, copied or written down, so it holds up against phishing. To create one, go to your account's passkey page and select Create a passkey . Only do it on devices you own; once a passkey exists, anyone who can unlock that device can get into your account.
Locking the front door doesn't help if someone already has a key, so check who and what is connected. Go to myaccount.google.com , open Security & sign-in and scroll down to the linked apps section, then select See all linked apps . You'll see the apps and sites you use Sign in with Google for, plus anything that has been given access to your account data. Anything you don't recognize or no longer use can go: select Remove access , then Confirm .
Next, look at Gmail itself. An attacker who gets in often changes a few quiet settings so they can keep reading your mail later. Open Gmail on your computer, click the gear icon in the top right and select See all settings . Then check for anything unfamiliar under automatic forwarding, filters, labels, scheduled emails, your vacation responder, and IMAP or POP access. Mail delegation, which lets someone else read, send and delete email in your account, has its own spot: go to the Accounts and Import tab and look under Grant access to your account . If a name is there that you didn't add, click Delete next to it. You can't manage delegates from the Gmail app, only on the desktop site. Automatic forwarding is the nasty one. It sends a copy of every new message, except spam, to another address, and you'd never notice. If you find a forwarding rule you didn't set up, change your password right away and turn it off.
The devices page is the other place to look. It lives in your Google Account, not in Gmail's settings: go to myaccount.google.com , open Security & sign-in (on a computer it may show up as just Security in the left-hand menu), find Your devices and select Manage all devices . You'll see everywhere you're signed in or have been in the last few weeks. Watch for a device you don't recognize, a location you weren't in or a browser you don't normally use. Take a moment to think about it, though: an airport, a library computer or a phone you recently reset can all look odd. If something really isn't yours, select the device and tap Sign out .
Once the settings are in place, a few habits keep them working. Keep two-step verification on, and never share a verification code with anyone. Google guarantees it won't call you to ask for one. Run Security Checkup again every now and then, since recommendations change and old devices and apps pile up.
In general, keep an eye out for any suspicious activity, or even lack of activity. For example, you stop receiving mail, friends tell you they got spam from you, there are emails sent that you didn't write or messages vanish from your inbox without landing in Trash. If any of that sounds familiar, change your password first, then work through the devices, apps and Gmail settings above.

articles.title_orig: A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase triggers online banking delays for major US banks
articles.title_zh: A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase triggers online banking delays for major US banks
articles.content_orig:
Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and U.S. Bank are reportedly among the major banks experiencing widespread online outages.
JPMorgan Chase’s systems were coming back online Monday after an hourslong nationwide outage left customers reporting trouble withdrawing funds and accessing their bank accounts.
The disruption was traced to a software release the bank rolled out earlier Monday that affected a subset of its systems, according to an FBI official. There was no indication of malicious or external cyber activity, the official said.
The impact was limited to JPMorgan Chase and transactions at other financial institutions in which JPMorgan Chase was a party, the official said.
The bank also said publicly that the incident was not malicious, and its systems were coming back online.
BANK OF AMERICA TO HIRE 1,000 MORE APPRENTICES, INVEST $150M IN WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT
After logging into the Chase app on November 16, during an online banking outage, one user reported seeing this error message. | Fox News
"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," Chase said. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible. This is a technical issue, not cyber-related."
Customers began reporting problems conducting transactions Monday morning. Chase earlier acknowledged an online banking issue in a response to a customer through its Chase Support account on X.
"We saw your post and want to reach out. I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking," Chase Support said. "Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience."
A teller at a Washington, D.C., Chase branch told FOX Business that in-store and online banking issues began around 10 a.m., and had been resolved just after 3 p.m. A branch manager said they had some glitches at the branch but can process most transactions there, on app and online. ATM machines were working as normal, the manager said.
At another branch, a Chase bank employee said the ATMs and banking app were working, but the computer system at the branch had "been up and down."
A JPMorgan Chase bank branch as customers experience disruptions due to a banking technology outage. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)
"It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," a company spokesperson said. "This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us."
Bank of America said its systems were operating normally.
"Bank of America systems have been operating normally today. Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information," the bank said in a statement.
LendingTree analyst Matt Schulz warns customers to watch for scammers exploiting confusion around reported Chase outages. His advice: verify updates directly with your bank and never share personal information with unsolicited callers or messages.
A spokesperson for US Bank also said its users were not experiencing issues.
"U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted," the spokesperson told Fox News. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delay."
BANK OF AMERICA UNVEILS $250B INITIATIVE TO MODERNIZE US INFRASTRUCTURE
PNC Financial Service and Wells Fargo told FOX Business they were not impacted by Monday's events.
Zelle, the digital payment network, said its system was working and operating as normal.
"Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should," the company said in a statement. "Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."
A JPMorgan Chase ATM is pictured outside the bank as technology disruptions impact banking services. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)
Zelle’s network operator is a company called Early Warning Services, which is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo, according to The Associated Press.
The outage happened just a week after an historic FAA ground stop of air travel nationwide Friday and a Microsoft Outlook email disruption Thursday.
'The Big Money Show' discusses customer reports of outages at major U.S. banks and examine the financial sector.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
Last week’s widespread Microsoft 365 outage was driven by three factors, including a software bug undetected since July, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said Monday.
The trend continued Monday evening, with United Airlines reporting a system-wide computer outage.
"We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience," the airlines told one person on X. "We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible. We appreciate your patience while we work through this."
United said the issue was resolved later Monday evening.
FOX Business' Ava Palschakov contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
articles.title_zh: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
articles.content_orig:
The number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and moral crisis, a landmark report into the problem will say later.
The 241-page report, by ex-Labour minister Alan Milburn, will set out a raft of recommendations for the government to consider.
Ahead of its publication, four young people who are not in education, employment or training - those dubbed as "Neets" - tell us why they can't get a job and how the government could help them get one.
Michael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.
Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people .
About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.
Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.
He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more.
"Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.
We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.
Lots of Neets receive Universal Credit. For under-25s, the standard rate is £338.58 a month , which Michael gets. For some people who cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness, an additional £217.26 to £429.80 per month may be available.
Ahead of the publication of his full review, it was reported that Milburn would recommend young people should no longer be able to claim those additional health-related benefits, as part of a major overhaul of the welfare system .
Michael acknowledges some young people may be "taking advantage" of the benefits system, but says most "just want the money to get by so they can get a job".
More recently, he has been doing shifts at the Merseyside Youth Centre's on-site cafe to gain more much-needed experience. His hope is to be in a steady job earning money this time next year, with space to have his own art studio one day.
"From three months ago I'm a different person," he says. "I can do stuff, keep going."
Maariyah, a 22-year-old history and politics graduate, finished her university course last summer. Her dream is to work in museums.
However, she is currently unemployed and looking for any paid job after working a temporary six-month contract for a housing association earlier this year.
She says she spends hours each day in her local library - where she feels more able to focus than she can at home - submitting at least 20 tailored job applications a week.
Those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualifications are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods - however, an estimated one in 10 Neets are university graduates .
Maariyah says she is applying for roles in retail and restaurants, alongside unpaid work experience opportunities in the heritage sector.
But she says she has also been rejected for voluntary roles because they had too many applicants, or because she does not have enough experience. "I'm actively going out of my way to do unpaid work, only to get rejected from these positions," she says.
Not hearing back from employers "happens so often now that's it's like second nature", she says, adding that she finds it frustrating that many of her applications are likely to be screened by AI before a real person sees them.
On the day we meet, Maariyah heads to the job centre for her Universal Credit appointment after a library job application session. She says she has noticed an improvement in the support she gets there since she first received the benefit in 2025.
This time, she will be getting some mandatory hospitality training, which she says she is "really glad" to have.
She feels there is a growing sense of disillusionment among others her age. Being on benefits has become normalised because it is so hard to find a job, she adds.
It makes her feel that going to a good university, getting certain grades and doing extracurricular activities "doesn't make a difference in the end".
"I would like employers to give young people a chance to gain experience and take a chance on hard-working people who at the end of the day want a job so that they can contribute to our economy and contribute to their own lives."
Matthieu, 19, from Edgware in north-west London, is autistic and currently volunteers at a gardening club and a computer repair shop.
We meet him in Finsbury Park, where he is helping to mulch some newly planted trees. Working in nature is calming, he says.
He is looking for work with the support of the charity Ambitious About Autism and his mentor, Annie. He previously did a year-long supported internship with the Whittington hospital.
Matthieu says speaking to people face-to-face there helped his confidence and he enjoyed being part of the team. At his family home, Matthieu's mentor Annie tells us that not having maths and English GCSE qualifications is a barrier to finding employment.
Matthieu says he's more of a manual worker and wants to work in a factory, warehouse or doing deliveries, so that he can contribute financially for his family.
Those with learning difficulties, including autism, make up an estimated 12% of Neets, DfE data shows. Milburn's interim report , which was published in the summer, said 45% of Neets reported having a disability. He said the situation for young disabled people was "devastating".
To make work accessible to him, Matthieu says he would need an employer to take their time with him. He says: "I don't learn that quickly." But he thinks it would be worth it.
"Honestly, you might be surprised what the people can do when you take the time with them and give them that chance," Matthieu says.
Many employers say they can not afford to do so following rises to National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage , which is increasing further as part of announcements made in October's Budget.
Some businesses have told the BBC they are struggling to provide new jobs for young people due to these changes, as well as other factors like rising energy bills.
Although finding work is hard, Matthieu says he remains hopeful because of the support from his internship and job coach.
Alex, 20, from St Helens, has been looking for work for a year. She struggles with anxiety and is looking for roles as a cleaner or in retail. She also shares caring responsibilities for her mum with her other family members.
We meet her at Spear, an employment and mindset coaching programme. Alex says her dream is to work with animals. She says she had been studying Level 3 animal management at college before dropping out last year because of her mental health.
"I was so burnt out," she says. "I was struggling to get out of bed, I couldn't do anything. I was dragging myself to college. I was like, 'No, I need to have a break for a bit and try and figure out what to do after that'."
Building up her resilience is something she now works on with a mentor, as well as job applications.
Alex says she is applying for "anything and everything" and wants to get off benefits. She is also currently receiving Universal Credit, which she says is "all the money that I've got until I get a job and I'm earning more".

articles.title_orig: Stock futures are little changed after Nvidia pressures tech to start the week: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures are little changed after Nvidia pressures tech to start the week: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures were little changed on Monday night, following a losing session as Nvidia once again dragged down the tech sector.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures inched up 8 points, or 0.02%. S&P 500 futures were up 0.06%, while Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.1%
Asia-Pacific markets opened lower Tuesday. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.76%, while the Topix declined 1.06%. South Korea's Kospi dropped 1.57%, while the small-cap Kosdaq lost 0.62%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 1.37%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell 1.17%, while mainland China's CSI 300 opened flat.
In regular U.S. trading, Nvidia shares pulled back 4.1%, as traders dumped the chipmaker ahead of its fiscal third-quarter report, due Tuesday after the bell. Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade fell as well, including AMD, Micron Technology and Sandisk.
"The tape feels increasingly fragile as Nvidia's AI premium continues to unwind and investors reassess the durability of the ecosystem built around its dominance," said Ben Emons, founder of FedWatch Advisors, in a note. "This backdrop has fueled the 'dispersion trade,' gradually eroding the extreme concentration that has defined the S&P 500 and Nasdaq."
Nvidia has been tumbling since last week. Jensen Huang resigned from the CEO post Thursday after reports emerged that he had multiple affairs , including one with an alleged Chinese spy . Further, the chipmaker's board of directors is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The stock has dropped almost 24% this month, putting it on pace for its biggest monthly decline since April 2022 — when it plunged 32%.
The 30-stock Dow on Monday slid more than 700 points, or 1.4%, while the S&P 500 lost 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.5%, its biggest one-day decline since Nov. 5.
On Tuesday, investors will pore through a slew of economic data, including October retail sales and import prices. On the earnings front, Disney and Home Depot are set to report before the opening bell.
Major Asian technology stocks fell on Tuesday after Nvidia shares extended losses in U.S. after hours trading, as uncertainty persisted over the chipmaker's leadership following Jensen Huang's departure. Nvidia is searching for a new CEO, while a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement has garnered more than 180,000 signatures.
Japan's SoftBank Group dropped 4.68% in early trading.
In South Korea, Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell 1.52% and 2.34%, respectively, dragging down the benchmark Kospi index.
Asia-Pacific markets opened lower on Tuesday.
Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.76%, while the Topix declined 1.06%. South Korea's Kospi dropped 1.57%, and the small-cap Kosdaq lost 0.62%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 1.37%.
Asia-Pacific markets were set to fall Tuesday, tracking sharp declines in U.S. equity benchmarks overnight.
Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 59,075 while in Osaka they were last at 59,200, compared with the index's previous close of 59,662.02.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 23,669 compared with the index's last close of 23,753.84.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 1.30% in early trade.
Wall Street's big bets came into view on Monday, as major investors released their latest 13F filings, which show where they put their money to work by the end of the third quarter.
Among the notable moves during the period were D1 Capital Partners increasing its positions in Lattice Semiconductor and chip materials supplier Qnity Electronics .
Check out CNBC Pro's roundup below for more.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures added 34 points, or 0.1%. S&P 500 futures gained 0.1%, and Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.2%.

articles.title_orig: FAA, Microsoft, banks: Why it feels like everything keeps breaking
articles.title_zh: FAA, Microsoft, banks: Why it feels like everything keeps breaking
articles.content_orig:
Thursday, it was Microsoft. Then, the nationwide ground stop.
Monday brought an outage that delayed many united flights. An outage at Chase impacted transactions at other banks like Bank of America, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
[DOWNLOAD: Free WSB-TV News app for alerts as news breaks ]
In the past week, four major technology breakdowns have disrupted how we work, how we travel, and even how we pay.
All involving the systems we depend on to make everyday life possible.
“It’s really scary because I wake up every day,” said resident Marquis Claiborne. “Everything’s online now, and I mean if everything’s shut down, you wouldn’t know what to do.”
In each case, there are no signs of a cybersecurity attack, but Emory professor Rajiv Garg says they expose a common vulnerability.
“This should act as a warning sign for every organization, because the infrastructure that the issues were seen in is a similar infrastructure for literally every organization,” said Garg.
Garg says as technology becomes more complex, even routine changes can create major problems.
He worries the push to roll out new technology faster is coming at the expense of testing and safeguards.
“The changes that are happening in the industry right now require more oversight, require more governance, require more guardrails in place,” said Garg. “While everyday people have little control over these breakdowns, they hope the companies learn from mistakes.”

articles.title_orig: U.S. moves to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips
articles.title_zh: U.S. moves to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips
articles.content_orig:
Data center company Megaspeed International's office in Singapore on Nov. 10, 2026. The company is suspected of selling remote access to U.S. AI chips to Chinese companies. A new Commerce Department rule would restrict that access. Taryn Ng/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.
The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.
The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.
The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security
However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.
The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.
Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.
Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.
"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.
Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.
The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."
Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.
The New York Times reported that Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.
"We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.title_zh: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.
In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.
"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.
