articles.title_orig: China is hosting the world's leaders in Shenzhen's AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
articles.title_zh: China is hosting the world's leaders in Shenzhen's AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
articles.content_orig:
At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream.
He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation.
Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans.
"We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here."
Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter.
The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.
Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition.
The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week.
And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
"Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs."
China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price.
A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.
The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits.
"Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name.
"Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything."
The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates.
Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies.
The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner.
"I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave.
To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire."
This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it.
Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all."
Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too.
This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences.
In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; £3.40).
On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan.
Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver.
She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk.
This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher."
Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan.
The wait for the elevator can take half an hour – wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy.
"The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings.
"The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hours… if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day."
An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before.
"We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries.
Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else."
Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.
"Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe.
Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay

articles.title_orig: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.title_zh: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.content_orig:
Scores of Bahrainis, mostly Shiite Muslim clerics according to a rights group, have been sentenced to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran’s Revolutionary Guards to undermine the state, prosecutors said on Monday.
Bahrain, a Shiite-majority country ruled by a Sunni Muslim family and home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet , has long been anxious about Iranian influence.
After Tehran began attacking Bahrain this year in response to the US-Israeli war on Iran, Bahrain accused it of fostering sedition, and launched a crackdown on Shiite clerics .
Between May and June, authorities arrested more than 50 clerics and religious orators, accusing them of trying to incite rebellion and overthrow the ruling order with help from Iran’s dominant Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Reuters reported this month.
The Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) said 64 defendants had been sentenced to life and five others to 15 years in prison after a trial that activists said began on July 5. It said 60 of the defendants were Shiite clerics.
A person close to the clerics’ defense teams described the verdicts as “worse than anything we imagined,” noting that not a single defendant had been acquitted. The person spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.
Some Shiites say they are oppressed for their beliefs, and in the early 2010s, the government jailed hundreds of mostly Shiite anti-government protesters.
Iran has rejected accusations of interference in Bahrain‘s internal affairs, but this year’s regional war has put authorities on edge once more.
“We are confronting an ideology that demands obedience to Iran’s leadership above Bahrain‘s sovereign authority,” Lieutenant General Tariq Al Hassan, head of Bahrain‘s Public Security Agency, said this month.
The High Criminal Court convicted all the defendants, some of whom were tried in absentia, of establishing and running a terrorist group linked to the IRGC that sought to overthrow the government, the prosecution said.
It did not specify the number of defendants or identify them as clerics or members of a particular sect, but accused them of raising funds without authorization and using mosques, religious sermons and charitable and educational institutions to promote allegiance to Iran’s supreme leader .
Some defendants were fined 100,000 Bahraini dinars ($265,000), and the court ordered the confiscation of more than 8 million Bahraini dinars ($21 million) for charitable purposes.
Among those sentenced to life imprisonment was Sheikh Isa Qassim, according to BIRD, who is widely regarded as the spiritual leader of Bahrain‘s Shiite community and has lived in Iran since 2018.
“To sentence a man in his late 80s, knowing that the conviction has no practical effect, is difficult to see as anything other than an act of retaliation,” said Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, BIRD’s director of advocacy.
Bahrain stripped Qassim of his citizenship in 2016, accusing him of promoting sectarianism, serving foreign interests and undermining loyalty to the state . The decision sparked protests and drew criticism from human rights groups and the US.
BIRD condemned the latest verdicts, citing allegations of torture, coerced confessions and restrictions on access to evidence. It said defendants had been interrogated without lawyers and pressured into signing statements they had not read.
Twenty rights groups, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, had previously raised concerns about the proceedings, citing allegations of torture, incommunicado detention and restrictions on access to evidence.
“This prosecution has torn religious leaders from their congregations and left families living under threats, fear and uncertainty,” said BIRD’s Alwadaei.
The prosecution said defendants’ legal rights had been upheld, with lawyers present and opportunities to examine evidence and question witnesses.

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Boosts Stake in Lennar, Doubling Down on Its U.S. Housing Bet
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Boosts Stake in Lennar, Doubling Down on Its U.S. Housing Bet
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway made several moves in the stock market during the third quarter, adding to key positions and trimming others.
The Omaha-based conglomerate, now led by CEO Greg Abel, increased its Delta Air Lines stake by 12%, scooping up 7.13 million shares. The position was worth $5.37 billion at the end of the third quarter.
Abel succeeded legendary investor Warren Buffett, 96, at the start of this year. Buffett continues to control roughly 13% of Berkshire common stock, Reuters said Monday, after the former CEO donated $5.5 billion to nonprofit foundations.
Berkshire boosted its stake in Delta as the Atlanta-based carrier's shares tumbled 11% in the third quarter, hurt by  rising jet fuel prices due to the U.S.-Iran war that pressured the entire airline industry. That marked the stock's worst quarterly performance since the first quarter of 2025, when it plunged 28%. Delta last month also cut its full-year earnings forecast , citing a surge in fuel costs.
To be sure, buying that dip has been a winning investment thus far. Delta is up 3.8% so far in the fourth quarter, while the S&P 500 has dropped 3.1%. Shares are also up nearly 15% over the past month.
Berkshire also trimmed its holding in Bank of America by nearly 6%, selling more than $1.6 billion worth of stock.
BofA was under pressure in the third quarter, falling more than 4%, as interest rates surged alongside stubbornly high inflation and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve monetary policy. At one point in September the 30-year Treasury bond yield surged above 5.6% to its highest level since 2002 .
Despite the share sale, Bank of America remains a top Berkshire Hathaway holding, with the conglomerate's stake valued at $24.8 billion at the end of the third quarter.
Berkshire also initiated a position in Bending Spoons and nearly doubled its stake in homebuilder Lennar in the latest quarter.

articles.title_orig: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
articles.title_zh: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
articles.content_orig:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.
During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.
“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”
The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.
Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.
The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.
The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.
Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said.
Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.
“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”
Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”.
Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.
Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

articles.title_orig: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
articles.title_zh: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump heads to Asia on Monday for high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine and smoothing over trade frictions with China. But the most tense meeting could take place aboard Air Force One.
Sequestered together on the journey across the world will be Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, whose long-running rivalry has recently spilled into the open.
Mr. Lutnick is under fire for slow-walking several measures aimed at clamping down on the supply of Nvidia chips to foreign data centers that serve Chinese clients. The controversy has put Mr. Lutnick at odds with Mr. Bessent, who has increasingly taken a hard line on China. While Mr. Lutnick has pushed for policies more favorable to Nvidia, Mr. Bessent has played the foil, going so far as to call for a dramatic shake-up of the company’s leadership.
The Treasury secretary traditionally manages America’s economic relationship with China. After spending much of last year trying to de-escalate tension between the world’s two largest economies over tariffs, Mr. Bessent has taken a more hawkish stance this year amid growing concern over the artificial intelligence race with China and risks that rogue Chinese A.I. technology could pose to the U.S. economy.
The internal clash over China policy has echoes of Mr. Trump’s first term, when the president’s economic advisers regularly argued about how forcefully to confront China over its trade practices. After Mr. Trump imposed steep tariffs on Chinese imports last year, Mr. Bessent called for de-escalation and helped broker a trade truce that stabilized the global economy.
But in recent months, the Trump administration has been frustrated that China has not lived up to its commitments for purchases of American farm products and to accelerate exports of its critical minerals, which are needed for making high-tech electronics and military equipment.

articles.title_orig: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.title_zh: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase says bank transactions are back to normal after outage online and at some branches
Chase Bank said transactions were posting normally Monday evening after a nationwide outage that had some customers reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds.
“Transactions are now posting normally,” a Chase spokesperson said around 6:30 p.m.
The outage began Monday morning, according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
Chase said at around 4 p.m. on X that “JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware system” and that it was working to resolve it.
The issues had been affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
The issue was not “cyber-related,” the bank said, and did not  impact the entire banking system. “Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”
The bank said that customers still had access to their accounts and funds, but some transactions were taking longer than normal.
Regulators were in touch with the big banks affected “immediately,” a person familiar with the situation said earlier Monday. They “quickly determined this was contained and service was already in process of restoration,” the person said then.
The issues at Chase were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week that have shaken public confidence in systems that tens of millions of Americans use every day. However, there is no evidence that these incidents are connected to one another.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade.
It was not immediately clear how many Chase accounts were affected by the glitch. The bank counts approximately 94 million customer relationships in the United States, with 5,000 physical branches and 15,000 ATMs.
By late afternoon Monday, several Chase bank branches in Manhattan appeared to be operating normally. Customers leaving a branch at 6th Avenue and W. 51st Street told NBC News they didn’t know there had been a problem until they arrived at the branch, where they were told by employees that they’d gotten there at just the right time.
“This is really retail banking,” and not tied to the rest of JPMorgan Chase, said a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The issues with Chase accounts also appeared to be preventing customers from transferring money via Zelle. A representative for the company said that the technical issues on its platform originated with Chase.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” the company told NBC News. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”
A representative for U.S. Bank confirmed that Zelle customers were experiencing issues.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted,” the spokesman said. “However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
A spokesperson for PNC Bank said it was “not experiencing any direct impact. We are aware of reports of transaction delays outside of the bank, but those appear to be resolving.”
Truist bank said its services “are operating normally,We continue to closely monitor our systems and are not aware of any broad service disruptions at this time.”
Customers at Wells Fargo also experienced delays, but the company did not provide a statement.
Citibank likewise declined to comment.
A spokesperson for Capital One said the bank “has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time.”
— WMAQ’s Lauren Stauffer and Leigh Lesniak contributed reporting from Chicago.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.
Kayla Steinberg is a producer at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.
articles.content_orig:
Nearly a decade ago, Elon Musk gave Tesla’s design team an unusual assignment: Build a sports car that can fly.
Mr. Musk brought in a small team of engineers from SpaceX, his rocket company, to lend a hand. Led by Bill Riley, SpaceX’s executive overseeing engineering on the rocket intended to land NASA astronauts on the moon, the team juggled their day jobs with outfitting a Roadster sports car with cold-gas thrusters, a technology more commonly found in rockets that has enough force to burst a human eardrum, according to three people familiar with the project.
This year, as engineers from both companies prepared for the car’s debut, they spent months putting it through its paces at SpaceX’s rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, the people said. In October, a driverless Roadster did a kick flip in midair, launching off a ramp more than 60 feet high.
This is “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company” Mr. Musk told the crowd.
The flying car demonstration offered a rare glimpse into how the world’s richest person has already created unusual cooperations between his two companies — which he now hopes to merge into a conglomerate valued at more than $3 trillion.
For years, Mr. Musk has quietly shuffled executives and engineers between Tesla and SpaceX to work on his passion projects, blurring the lines between the two, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential business matters. The arrangements highlight how Mr. Musk treated the huge companies as interchangeable parts of a single empire, long before shareholders have been asked to vote on combining them.

articles.title_orig: Ousted President Is Moved From Comfort to Military Prison
articles.title_zh: Ousted President Is Moved From Comfort to Military Prison
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay’s former President Santiago Pena has been transferred to a military prison on a judge’s orders, following reports that he was granted special amenities while awaiting trial for a financial corruption scandal.
On Monday, Judge Osmar Legal ordered Pena to be moved from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital city of Asuncion.
There, media reports indicated he had a large dining room, furnishings, a private gym and a bathroom, sparking public backlash.
His new lodgings are inside Vinas Cue military prison. Pena, however, is to be held separately from the facility’s other prisoners for his safety.
Allegations against the former president are at the centre of a corruption scandal related to the collapse of a major financial lender, Ueno Bank, used by more than half of the country’s adult population.
The political crisis erupted into the public spotlight on November 3, when Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno after declaring it insolvent.
In doing so, it froze account activity for nearly three million people. In the months before its collapse, Ueno held roughly $850m in public funds, including money for retirement pensions.
The scandal led to the end of Pena’s presidency. A member of the conservative Colorado Party, a leading force in Paraguay’s politics, Pena saw his political allies distance themselves from him in the wake of the lender’s collapse.
His attempts to resign were rejected, as Paraguay’s Congress instead pursued impeachment proceedings against him. He was removed from office on November 6.
As criminal investigations unfolded, scrutiny fell on Pena’s role as a shareholder in Ueno’s parent company. Pena has denied wrongdoing and said he sold his shares in 2025.
Prosecutors, however, have accused Pena of using his position in office to direct public funds to the bank while it made insider loans to owners.
He faces charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Angry protests accompanied Pena’s removal , and he was ordered to be held in pretrial detention.
His former vice president, Pedro Alliana , has since been sworn in to lead Paraguay’s executive branch.
In a news conference on Monday, Alliana said he had dismissed a military official, Colonel Jose David Daiub, accused of giving Pena special treatment while in detention.
“Our priority is to guarantee the country’s stability, restore confidence, and provide concrete and rapid solutions,” said Alliana.
Paraguayans, he added, “deserve to know the truth”. Pena’s transfer to a military prison came on his 48th birthday.

articles.title_orig: United Airlines says it resolved a "widespread system outage," days after nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: United Airlines says it resolved a "widespread system outage," days after nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
United Airlines on Monday said a widespread system outage that delayed flight departures is over.
In a statement early Monday evening, the airline said it had resolved a technology issue linked to the problem, which came on the heels of a nationwide FAA ground stop.
While some flights were delayed, the company said, there was no impact on flights in progress or on United Express flights.
United announced the outage roughly an hour earlier, just before 5 p.m.
The union representing United pilots said in a statement that the outage had affected multiple pilot-facing applications, including crew communications and messaging systems, as well as the airline’s ability to provide final aircraft weight information for departing flights.
The union said it was working with management to better understand the scope of the disruption. Pilots had been advised to follow procedures in the flight operations manual, according to the statement.
A passenger on a United flight bound for Hong Kong told NBC News that a pilot announced that they’d been unable to get performance data for takeoff because of an IT issue. The pilot said they planned on doing “old school” calculations so they could take off, according to the passenger, Halina Eth.
In another announcement, the pilot said that systems were back online and there was a “very narrow window of opportunity to get this flight in the air,” according to a video shared with NBC News.
The issue did not appear to be related to technical issues that prompted the ground stop that halted air travel across the United States for more than four hours Friday evening.
Other airlines did not appear to be affected by Monday’s United issue.
It’s the latest system relied on by millions of Americans to falter . Earlier Monday, JPMorganChase said a technical issue was causing some banking transactions to be delayed for both its own customers and others.
Late Friday, the FAA was forced to issue a nationwide ground stop after a fiber upgrade crashed a critical communication system. By Monday, air travel in the U.S. was largely returning to normal after a chaotic weekend for travelers, crews and airlines.
And last week, Microsoft Outlook went down due to what the tech giant said was a “bug” and overwhelmed servers.
While there is no evidence that any of the issues are related, they seem to be fulfilling concerns about America’s overreliance on aging infrastructure. They’re also occurring against a backdrop of warnings about AI risks and cyberattacks, stoking fears that wider problems may be afoot.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Interim CEO Kress prepares for Q3 earnings, with Huang reportedly planning comeback
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Interim CEO Kress prepares for Q3 earnings, with Huang reportedly planning comeback
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said he would be open to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returning to the company he resigned from last week amid the fallout from an extramarital relationship he had with an alleged Chinese spy.
"I think he learned a big lesson," Trump said of Huang when asked by reporters on Monday whether he wants to see the company co-founder reinstated as CEO.
Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House before departing for a trip to Asia, downplayed national security concerns stemming from the affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company that U.S. officials suspect of having funneled Nvidia's advanced chips to China.
"It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. Trump is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.
The president told reporters he is not planning to replace Howard Lutnick as commerce secretary after questions arose about the Cabinet member's handling of export controls involving Nvidia's advanced chips.
Republican and Democratic members of Congress have raised concerns about the national security implications of the episode after it was revealed that Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in the 1990s, had an extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading global supplier of advanced artificial intelligence chips.
Critics argue the affair could jeopardize the U.S.' global dominance in AI and that it raises questions about influence exerted by Nvidia's Huang on regulators and lawmakers as he opposed export controls that limited the sale of the company's chips to Chinese firms.
The New York Times reported Tuesday that the U.S. believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and that Secretary of State Marco Rubio alerted Trump to the situation aboard Air Force One in May before Jensen Huang joined the president on a flight to China.
The Washington Post reported Friday that Rubio had issued a memo to Trump warning the president about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
But Trump on Monday said "I haven't heard that" when asked about Rubio's warning.
"I don't know that she is a spy. Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said, of Alice Huang. "I don't know that she was a spy at all."
Trump also attempted to defuse tension bubbling within his Cabinet between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Lutnick.
Axios reported last week that Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China,  prompting a Situation Room confrontation between the men. Both are traveling with Trump on Monday to Asia, as is Rubio.
And Bessent, in an appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday, seemed to express frustration at Lutnick for not putting Megaspeed, Alice Huang's former company, on a Commerce Department list of companies that pose national security concerns.
The departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the 'entity list' for months," Bessent said.
Trump acknowledged on Monday that Lutnick might have delayed putting Megaspeed on the list but defended his rationale as essential for diplomacy.
"He was doing that because you could have — if you didn't delay it, If you didn't do something — you could have a blow-up with China," Trump said. "We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I'll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides."
Trump, who previously had said he did not plan to raise the Jensen Huang issue with Xi when they meet this week, said he may do so. He also said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.
As Trump downplays concerns about fallout from the affair and advanced chips finding their way to China, Capitol Hill leaders are taking a different approach .
A spokesperson for House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told CNBC "negotiations are still going" about Jensen Huang testifying before a trio of House committees.
Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford, R-Ark., had given Huang a deadline of 8 p.m. ET Friday to respond to their request to appear before the committees. Mast has said he would subpoena the former CEO if he doesn't accept the invitation voluntarily.

articles.content_orig:
President Trump’s trip to Asia this week will largely be seen as a test of American power in the main region where the United States and China compete for influence.
His meetings in Manila and Shenzhen, China, will be scrutinized for shifts on trade and security. Deals he might strike with Beijing — plus a gathering with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia — will put the world’s great-power contest on display, as all three seek to show strength.
But Asia is not just a theater of competition. Many countries in the region have become wealthier, more technologically advanced and increasingly interconnected . Especially now, as China’s military becomes more threatening and the United States less reliable, they are hedging against greatness and relying more on neighbors.
Asian students and workers are moving to neighboring states. Countries with expanding defense industries are selling weapons to new partners. Nations that compete for high-tech investment are even making plans to cooperate on energy and cybersecurity .
“They’re all looking at what more they can do together when the great powers are behaving so badly,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam and adjunct professor of geopolitics at Fulbright University in Ho Chi Minh City. “If you’re a middle power, you’re thinking ‘I need more options.’”
Here are a few numbers that provide a sense of what the region contributes to the global economy, and how its nations are becoming more bound together to shape the world.

articles.title_orig: U.S. is absolutely slowing China down in AI chip race, says China Beige Book CEO
articles.title_zh: U.S. is absolutely slowing China down in AI chip race, says China Beige Book CEO
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
articles.title_zh: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
articles.content_orig:
By SAM MERRIMAN, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 18:54 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 18:54 EST, 16 November 2026
The author of a landmark review into NHS gender services on Monday night withdrew her support for Labour 's controversial ban on conversion therapy.
Baroness Cass warned the proposed ban would have 'serious unintended consequences', adding: 'I can't support the Bill in its current form.'
The Draft Conversion Practices Bill, which covers England and Wales, would outlaw 'abusive' attempts to change someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
Perpetrators who utilised abusive therapy to attempt to change gay and transgender people's sexuality or gender identity could, under the Bill, face five-year prison sentences and unlimited fines.
Baroness Cass on Monday revealed that a supportive comment from her in a government press release launching the Bill was made before she had seen its full details – and she was given only 15 minutes' notice before her comment was published.
She told a parliamentary committee scrutinising the Bill: 'I hadn't actually seen [it] and said that I couldn't give a statement until I had.
'Unfortunately, I was not sent the Bill until about 15 minutes before they wanted the press comment.'
Labour had been relying on Baroness Cass's comments in support of the Bill and her change in position will be seen as a serious setback for ministers.
Baroness Cass warned the proposed ban would have 'serious unintended consequences', adding: 'I can't support the Bill in its current form' (file image)
Following Baroness Cass's 2024 Review into NHS gender services at the Tavistock clinic, then-health secretary Wes Streeting banned puberty blockers for under-18s indefinitely over the 'unacceptable safety risk' they pose to children.
There have been warnings that parents who have normal conversations with their children, or refuse to fund gender surgery, could be criminalised by the new Bill.
It would also make it illegal to tell someone who identifies, for example, as a cat, that they are human.
Baroness Cass said she had based her initial support on talks with ministers about 'the principles of how the Bill would operate', but that after considering Labour's proposals she did not 'think that it is anywhere near tight enough to avoid serious unintended consequences'.
Baroness Cass, now an independent adviser to the Department of Health and Social Care, warned that the Bill could have 'chilling effects' for healthcare workers who have difficult conversations with gender-questioning young people as part of their jobs.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI sued by California over 80 ‘loss of control’ incidents
articles.title_zh: OpenAI sued by California over 80 ‘loss of control’ incidents
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday Nov. 16, 2026. In the complaint, California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. California Department of Justice/Screenshot by NPR hide caption
California sued OpenAI Monday, alleging that the frontier AI company failed to protect the public from its systems' advanced cyber capabilities. The lawsuit stems from OpenAI's agents' attack on open-source software platform Hugging Face over the summer but also touches on a wide range of other related incidents tied to the company's agents acting without authorization.
"Just because the technology is new or rapidly evolving doesn't mean the people behind it are above the law," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards." The lawsuit cited potential concerns about cyberattacks "on power grids, emergency infrastructure, hospital systems, and financial institutions."
In the complaint , California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. The state said the company admitted to the attorney general's office that "it lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing."
That number is higher than what OpenAI has so far disclosed publicly and more than what outside researchers have independently discovered, but OpenAI has otherwise provided little information, California said. The state also accused OpenAI of poor security practices, stonewalling the state's investigation into the company and discouraging employees from speaking up about safety.
In a statement to NPR, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab" and that the company has "engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."
After the most notorious of cyber incidents involving OpenAI's agents – the attack on Hugging Face over the summer – the company admitted that it did not monitor its agents in ways its own researchers deemed important. Since then, outside researchers as well as OpenAI itself have found more incidents in which AI agents have interacted with websites and communicated with each other on the internet in ways that OpenAI did not intend. The lawsuit mentions these events as well as other incidents that OpenAI started disclosing voluntarily to the public.
Other AI companies have also had to wrestle with their systems behaving in unexpected and undesirable ways. Anthropic and Meta have both said they found that their AI systems have hacked into places they shouldn't have. Major AI companies have since signed onto an agreement organized by the White House to develop AI responsibly, but the agreement is nonbinding.
Drawing from reports including from OpenAI's own disclosures, California alleges that the top AI company has engaged in unfair competition and created a public nuisance. It asked the court to stop the company from further engaging in such activities and order it to pay monetary damages.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi Meet This Week: Could Footwear See U.S., China Pause Trade Truce Extension a Second Time?
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi Meet This Week: Could Footwear See U.S., China Pause Trade Truce Extension a Second Time?
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue was driven by China last year: report
articles.title_zh: More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue was driven by China last year: report
articles.content_orig:
More than 20% of Nvidia’s revenue last fiscal year was generated by China – a massive cut that shows the size of the chip giant’s murky business with the US adversary, according to a report.
Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang helped power an ecosystem in which it sold its most powerful chips to east Asian data centers that in turn powered tech offered by Chinese tech giants like Alibaba, according to reports.
Such deals drove more than a fifth of Nvidia’s revenue during the previous fiscal year, according to Culper Research, the short-selling firm that originally called out Nvidia’s China issues in May.
Huang’s efforts to supply China with key AI tech showered Nvidia with an eye-watering $12.4 billion in revenue in the six months through July 26 of this year, or 7% of its global revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal, which added that countless more billions of dollars could ultimately trace back to Chinese customers.
The dealings were a workaround to US export controls that sought to keep Nvidia’s top-of-the-line tech out of the hands of Chinese firms – and proved to be a cash cow for the chip giant, according to the Journal report .
As the full extent of Nvidia’s lucrative China business emerges, the Commerce Department announced Monday it is nixing the provision that has allowed Chinese firms to skirt export controls on American AI chips.
Despite US export restrictions that have thwarted US chip sales directly to China, Nvidia sold chips to firms that set up data centers in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia which then sold the computing power to Chinese tech giants.
Some of those firms – including Singapore-based Megaspeed , which was led by Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy and mistress to the former Nvidia CEO – have even been suspected of forwarding chips directly to China.
Between March 2024 and June 2025, Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion worth of top-of-the-line Nvidia chips to companies in China, according to the WSJ report.
Shipment records show orders for several hundred thousand of the type of chips that US regulations intended to keep out of Chinese hands. The report notes that records don’t specify how many of the chips were actually delivered or where they originated from.
The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule that seeks to close a loophole that Chinese firms have used to lease Nvidia’s advanced computing power by going through data centers in third-party countries, according to a Monday press release .
A license will now “be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion,” according to the new rule .
In a Sunday letter addressed to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington – the top Dem on the Senate Commerce Committee – urged the Commerce secretary to reinforce export controls on the sale of AI chips to China.
Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance have “used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models,” she wrote. “These companies are exploiting a loophole in US export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People’s Republic of China].
Nvidia says it works to prevent smuggling.
Megaspeed told the Journal that it conducts lawful business and designs its supply chain to comply with US export controls. Megaspeed added that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it has retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation.
Lutnick has come under fire since the revelations with critics on Capitol Hill questioning why the agency didn’t blacklist Megaspeed. Lutnick – whose job is speculated to be in jeopardy – is set to testify before the Senate about his agency’s handling of AI chip export controls.

articles.title_orig: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
articles.title_zh: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
articles.content_orig:
The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX’s ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch.
However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle?
The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won’t launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA’s lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth.
Given what is known publicly, and what Ars has heard privately, here are some educated guesses about all of this.
The first thing we can say for sure is that all estimates of human spaceflight on Starship should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt, including those in this article. Putting humans on any space vehicle is a difficult and time-consuming task, even outside of the requirements that NASA would impose for its astronauts.
The original target for launching humans on Starship (then known as the Interplanetary Transport System) set a decade ago was 2024. That was for a Mars mission. Then, in 2018 , SpaceX announced a lunar flyby mission on Starship with a target launch in 2023. This dearMoon mission was canceled in 2024. In 2022, SpaceX and Dennis Tito announced a lunar flyby mission later in the 2020s.
More recently, according to sources, SpaceX has been telling individuals interested in launching on Starship that it could begin offering flights by 2029. I probably would not put too much stock in this date.
All of this is to say, we cannot learn much from history other than to deeply discount any public launch dates on Starship for humans.
Most likely, the first humans to fly on Starship in space will do so after launching from Earth inside the NASA Orion spacecraft. Once in orbit they will then dock with Starship before transiting to the Moon, landing there in Starship, launching from the Moon back to Orion, and then returning to Earth inside NASA’s spacecraft.
NASA signed an agreement with SpaceX to develop Starship as this “Human Landing System” in 2021, with a lunar landing targeted for 2024. To no one’s surprise, this target has moved to 2028, and there remains considerable uncertainty about the viability of this date.
Nevertheless, the success of Saturday’s tower catch should help propel the Starship program toward a higher launch cadence, which is essential for lunar missions. It therefore seems plausible, but not certain, that humans could land on the Moon inside Starship before the end of this decade.
Again, how soon SpaceX achieves this target will depend upon its prioritization of a Human Landing System, among its other major goals to accomplish with Starship. At this point, SpaceX appears to be more focused on revenue-generating activities such as launching Starlink, and eventually, Starmind data center satellites.
Much has been made about the fact that Starship does not have a launch abort system—a feature of most human spacecraft that allows a crew vehicle to be rapidly pulled away from an exploding rocket.
This may not matter should SpaceX conduct its own human spaceflight missions. Unlike NASA, which imposes detailed human-rating requirements on vehicles carrying its astronauts, the Federal Aviation Administration does not certify commercial spacecraft as safe for passengers, instead operating under a regulatory framework that emphasizes informed consent and protection of the uninvolved public. Should SpaceX reach the point where it can launch Starship reliably, it will have the confidence it needs to press forward with human flights. Conceivably, this could happen within a few years.
According to potential customers, SpaceX is developing variants of the Human Landing System Starship for human flights, potentially carrying a few dozen people to the Moon. And such a prospect is tantalizing, for the interior of Starship’s pressurized cabin is almost unimaginably large for a spacecraft. A single Starship lunar lander has a pressurized habitable volume greater than the comparable volume of the International Space Station. This would be extraordinary.
Yet it is not a simple step to go from the current lunar lander design to an Earth lander. NASA’s lunar lander will never need to experience the tremendous heating of atmospheric reentry or perform the dramatic flip maneuver and propulsive landing that Starship uses to return home. Certifying those capabilities for human passengers, particularly on a vehicle without a traditional launch escape system, is an entirely different challenge.
Moreover, building a commercial human spaceflight business on Starship would be time-consuming and would likely not be nearly as profitable as launching Starlink satellites into space. And the risk is far greater—spaceflight remains dangerous, and the loss of a human crew would be a major negative for a publicly traded company. On the other hand, losing dozens of Starlink satellites on an errant launch would be a blip.
Despite Starship’s enormous theoretical capacity, SpaceX has also shown little interest in developing it as a crew transportation vehicle for commercial space stations in the near term. Several private space station operators have approached SpaceX about the possibility of Starship bringing astronauts to and from their stations. SpaceX indicated it was not interested.
Putting all of this together, I would not expect humans to land on Earth in Starship before 2030, and plausibly not until at least the mid-2030s.

The rapid proliferation of hyperscale data centres (HDCs) in the USA—mainly driven by the adoption of artificial intelligence—has raised concerns about this industry’s carbon footprint. We compiled facility-level information on 403 US hyperscale data centres operating between May 2024 and April 2025 and estimated their electricity consumption, electricity sources and attributable CO 2 emissions. Across facility-load scenarios, these HDCs consumed approximately 68–99 TWh of electricity and were associated with approximately 21–31 million metric tons of CO 2 under a location-based, total-output balancing-authority attribution method. Under the central scenario, HDC electricity demand was approximately 82 TWh, corresponding to about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption, and attributable CO 2 emissions were approximately 25.7 Mt. Roughly 54% of attributed generation was supplied by fossil-fuel sources. The HDC electricity-weighted total-output carbon intensity was approximately 314 gCO 2 kWh −1 , compared with a US total-output average of approximately 348 gCO 2 kWh −1 . Our approach provides a facility-resolved attributional framework for assessing the carbon footprint of hyperscale data centres using plant-level electricity-generation and emissions data.

They are available through the public reproducibility repository 46 . The repository exports, rather than the separate visualization interface, constitute the authoritative public data products for the revised analysis. Because the underlying facility data are protected by a data-use agreement, raw facility identifiers, addresses, coordinates and commercially sensitive facility attributes are not publicly released. The complete facility-level map-generation workflow requires authorized access to those inputs. Access to facility-level map coordinates remains subject to provider authorization and the data-use agreement; public aggregate files do not substitute for the restricted facility-level observations. Source data are provided with this paper.
All code used to estimate HDC power capacity, evaluate the capacity model, compute electricity use and emissions, validate public aggregate exports and reproduce manuscript-facing numerical results is publicly available in the public reproducibility repository 46 . A tagged snapshot corresponding to the Round 3 reproducibility materials is available as version v0.3.1-round3-final 47 . The repository contains: (1) the fully specified scikit-learn capacity-model pipeline, including disclosed predictors, preprocessing, effective hyperparameters, software version and evaluation metrics; (2) a non-identifying 403-row synthetic facility fixture with six missing power-capacity values; (3) a deterministic public synthetic split artefact at results/tables/synthetic_validation/splits.json , together with random and grouped validation outputs; (4) REPRO.md , documenting the validation sample, explicit imputation indicator, software versions, restricted-data workflow and emissions-accounting conventions; (5) scripts/reproduce_model.py , which regenerates the public synthetic validation outputs and writes the deterministic split artefact; (vi) the total-output emissions-attribution workflow using EPA eGRID2023 Revision 2; (7) denominator-audit, plant-inventory, public-export, restricted-data and manuscript-output validation scripts and (8) aggregate state- and balancing-authority-level exports used to verify the headline results. The public synthetic and aggregate materials allow external researchers to execute the capacity-model validation workflow, verify the emissions denominator, reproduce headline scenario totals, sum the public regional exports and run the repository tests without access to restricted facility records.

articles.title_zh: Chase customers report widespread online banking problems
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase reports an issue that appears to be causing outages to online and in-person banking services
An issue with Chase banking services led to some customers of that institution and others reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds Monday.
The issues appeared to be affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” Chase said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The issues at Chase were caused by a “technical bug, not a cyber issue,” according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
A Zelle representative said that a technical issue on its platform originated with Chase.
“This is a Chase issue,” a Zelle spokesman told NBC News. “You need to speak to them.”
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
The outages were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade .
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s stock extends declines following harsh words from the U.S. government
articles.content_orig:
In the past week, shares of Nvidia ( NVDA -3.96% ) have been in a downward spiral. News that Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO and has been involved in multiple affairs, one of which may involve a Chinese spy, has significantly weighed on the company's valuation.
The stock has fallen so sharply that it is now trading at levels it hasn't been at since June of last year. Given how sudden and significant the sell-off has been, many investors are likely worried that there may still be worse to come. Could the tech stock fall to $100?
Image source: Getty Images.
When things are going well for a stock, the temptation is to assume it'll only continue to do well and rise higher. And when things are going poorly, many investors may fear that things will only get worse. Both outlooks, however, can be incredibly irrational. Sooner or later, the excitement or panic fades, and the stock stabilizes and may even end up going in the opposite direction.
Due to its sharp decline, Nvidia's stock is now trading at around 20 times its trailing earnings. And on a forward basis, based on analyst expectations of future earnings, its forward price-to-earnings multiple is just ten. That's an incredibly low valuation given that the S&P 500 average is a forward earnings multiple of 19.
The stock is already heavily discounted , and for a more significant decline to take place, one that takes it to $100, that would likely require there to be much more negative news around the tech business. And there would also likely need to be an all-out crash in the tech sector.
NASDAQ · As of 2:56 PM ET 11/16/26
The last time Nvidia's stock was at around $100 was after the Liberation Day tariffs were announced in April 2025. Global trade uncertainty weighed on not only Nvidia but the markets as a whole, and unless there's that kind of uncertainty and fear rattling the markets once more, I wouldn't expect Nvidia to fall to those levels anytime soon.
Nvidia is already an incredibly cheap-looking stock to buy given how well it has performed in recent years. Waiting for an even lower price could be risky for investors, because the risk is that it may never reach those levels; buying the stock now may be a much better move than holding out hope that it will fall even further.

articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub
articles.title_zh: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub
articles.content_orig:
Five European countries unveiled plans on Monday to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.
Under the planned scheme — which is still being negotiated with Rwanda — Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands would send people to a center where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said.
“I think it will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges of illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told a press conference in Vienna with her Austrian counterpart and ministers from the countries involved.
The five countries have been working towards a deal for a so-called return hub for several months, officials have said — part of a broader push inside the European Union to increase deportation s and curb irregular migration.
With elections approaching in several EU countries, centrist governments have been toughening immigration policies to try to counter growing public support for far-right parties.
In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.
The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.
Although officials say such a hub would only handle about 100 people at a time, the countries championing it say it would send an important signal that they hope will discourage would-be migrants from making the often perilous journey to Europe.
The project follows the approval of the EU’s new Return Regulation, designed to speed up deportations.
The scheme differs from Britain’s abandoned Rwanda deportation plan in that it would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the European Union, rather than those whose claims are still being processed.
Rwanda has positioned itself as a destination for migrants whom Western countries want to remove, despite longstanding concerns about its own human rights record.
“Under this partnership, Rwanda would provide a second chance to people who no longer have the legal right to remain in the partner countries,” Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said on Monday.
Rwanda was not looking to be paid for the arrangement, but partner countries would meet the cost of relocation and the integration of any who chose to stay in Rwanda, he added.
Veteran President Paul Kagame won praise from Western and regional leaders for helping end Rwanda’s 1994 genocide and rebuilding the East African country into a destination for investment.
However, critics accuse his government of suppressing dissent and supporting rebels alleged to have committed killings, rapes and other abuse in neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo. Rights advocates also point to restrictions on political freedoms and free speech.
Freedom House rates it “Not Free” and cites what it describes as the suppression of political dissent through surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and torture.
“There is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” Amnesty International said in a statement on Monday.
The United States last year began transferring migrants to Rwanda under an agreement allowing it to deport up to 250 people.
Britain abandoned its own plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda after it was ruled unlawful by the country’s Supreme Court in 2023. Kigali sought a £50 million ($63.6 million) payment after the UK scheme was scrapped.
During a September visit to Kigali, two European Parliament lawmakers were shown facilities earmarked for Britain’s abandoned scheme that could potentially house migrants transferred from EU countries, including a hotel.
